Had him for first sim - helpful and friendly guy. Gives some pretty good hints & tips. Grades fairly but don't expect inflated grades

2103-Nice guy. I came prepared and had questions from previous sims, He liked that. He would talk to me looking at my name tag so much so i thought I was jacked up but he just looks down when talking. Don't be off put. .

2103: Very nice and helpful. He talked a lot during the brief and would stop me at different times during checklists when there are multiple things to consider before proceeding (such as after an aborted start and when the NATOPS says you can and can't do the toring run procedure to attempt another start). Didn't actually simulate aircraft departing prepared surface, just discussed it during the brief and after aborting the takeoff. Had lots of extra time so he walked me through the radio calls for going from NA to Evergreen and then how to use the FMS to return to base. Overall a great instructor and pretty simple sim.

C2103- Nice guy. Wants you to brief concisely. Will press you to get you to think and to get an understanding of how much you really know. Will throw some tricks at you in the sim but nothing unfair. He wants you to catch them and is happy when you do. Cares about you being "eager to learn" and will do that by keeping you on your toes.

Very helpful instructor who has interesting but helpful ways of coaching/helping you remember certain techniques. For I2101 he essentially led the brief, so if you've prepared, make sure you try to beat him to the number he's about to tell you or the procedure he's about to go over (in a professional way), in order to prove you did actually prepare and know your stuff. Very nice guy overall and incredibly easy to work with and learn from.

Had him for a warm-up sim so take it for what it is but he was incredibly helpful with all the things i wanted to work on. Very mellow and level but will get a little excited when he is coaching you through a maneuver or the pattern. He had lots of awesome flying experience in the coast guard flying in Nor Cal and Alaska. Also ask him about the time he hit a deer on the runway, great story and he is an awesome story teller.
C2103. Helpful, but it seemed like he was trying to get me as flustered as possible

During the sim. Felt like I was doing terrible, but he said I actually did well. Very particular about being absolutely verbatim using the Hollywood Checklist, and doing the challenge, completing the action, and then stating the a response. Nice during brief and debrief.

Had him for C2102 and I2103 with pretty different results. Was very affable during the brief and debrief both times and really babied me through putting on the harness, putting away the PCL, etc. Once we got in the cockpit his demeanor changed. VERY intense about Hollywood being verbatim in early sims. Got on to me multiple times for not properly pluralizing commands ("MFDS", "PMU Fail/PMU Status messages"). Told me he "didn't want to hear that shit" when I was talking through the lights during the lamp test. Really tried to stress me out and get me flustered during start up. For the BIs, he will talk through his scan with his terms while doing maneuvers. My scan had been working really well for me and I found it really difficult to think over his talking, but ultimately it went well because the only parameters he cared about during the maneuvers were the ones he was saying. So while my heading was re off than normal, he didn't seem to mind if the ones he emphasized were on point.

C2202. Very pleasant instructor to have, can tell he loves his job. I studied the briefing guide pretty hard but he asked alst 0 questions in the brief related to the briefing guide. Instead, he dug very deep into systems and asked me a lot of systems questions. He didn't have a big problem with me getting most of those questions wrong but i felt dumb. Actual sim went well, make sure you actually bother to look at your engine instruments before you call them "checked" as he messed with them a lot.

Had him for C2101, he was a good instructor to have. Definitely check messages before silencing alarms like said above, and also make sure you know all the specifics from the Hollywood. If you get through the checklist fast he'll show you how to do some maneuvers in the air and give you tips which is cool. Know your stuff and you'll get a fair grade.

Really nice guy, knows his stuff and wants to help you. Come prepared for the brief and you'll be set. He's calm during the brief and that makes you calm. He'll give helpful pointers during the sim that make a huge difference. He's really good at seeing where a student struggles whether its with a maneuver or a procedure and he will give you advice you don't hear anywhere else.
C2102 - Fun, good guy. Will help you as much as he can if you show you read and are willing and want to learn. Will throw random errors at you so keep alert on your EICAS.

I2102- This guy is great. He will ask you questions about the brief so be prepared. Will also talk with you and get to know you a little as well. He has a great demeanor and a very calming presence. Helps a ton in the sim with little tips and tricks from his experience as an aviator, but will expect you to know the procedures execute them and then help you. Does NOT walk you through everything so be ready.

C3203 - He did not ask questions related to the briefing guide. Very nice guy, but I did not jive well with him. He threw a lot of curve balls and would excessively coach you to the point it was confusing and distracting. Very calm demeanor but I could tell he was getting irritated. Maybe he's not a rning person. Just be prepared for a variety of situations and take a minute to evaluate the situation and act. Very NATOPS/FTI centric

C2102: Very nice and calm guy as said above with a classic old-school sense of hur. Will ask a couple briefing guide type questions but other than that he leads the brief; he really gets into the systems particularly regarding battery vs. external powers start so study that for the early sims if that is the case for you. He does throw a couple of curveballs so keep your eyes on the EICAS and FIRE light. Really good at gauging how much talking he needs to do; if you aren't prepared, he will talk a lot. If you know your shit, he will let you go about your routine until you make a mistake, making for an efficient sim, and your grades will reflect it.

I2104 - During the brief we just talked about general aviation, though I2104 is basically nothing new from previous sims so that could've had something to do with it. He won't talk much during the sim, which can be a godsend if you're someone who's easily distracted by instructors who ramble while you're trying to focus on flying or a death sentence if you don't know your procedures for the maneuvers you're completing. Overall very chill, and grades relatively generously. Got a late start on our sim but still ended up with 10 minutes of free time which he used to denstrate maneuvers from the next block, so if you have him and finish early he'll probably ve on to the next sim. Would 100% take him again, but don't expect him to offer a ton of feedback or technique like other instructors

Brush up on your systems knowledge before the brief. I had him for C2102 and he asked a lot of questions about the fuel system, toring runs, how the starter works, and limits on the battery. Has over 4000 hours in ejection seat aircraft and takes wearing the gear and strapping in very seriously. I learned a lot from him on this and now I feel very confident about strapping in. Overall, I can tell he is there to instruct and make us better. I'd like to have him again
Definitely brush up on systems knowledge, was involved in testing the T-6 and damn near wrote the book, so he'll dig pretty deep. I had
him for 2201, and he told me he'd basically pitch me all the EPs so none were big surprises, but he still gave me an engine fail after takeoff without warning and said he wanted to see if I'd eject.
Really nice guy, but goes way into the weeds. He'll over saturate you before you even get into the cockpit, and then wonder why you're garbage BAW. Had him for the crosswind sim and I2201.

Very nice, flew Prowlers and then was a test pilot. Had him for C2101, and he went incredibly in depth with the fuel system. Overall, great instructor. He is chill as fuck as long as you are bringing a good attitude to the table.

C2202. Easily my favorite instructor so far. He is an absolute knowledge powerhouse. He asks a lot of systems questions, and even some NATOPS EP knowledge that isn't boldface or in the briefing guide. He helped me walk through any questions I had. He was a test pilot for the T6B and a ton of hours in it, as well as in the F16. Funny, easy to talk to, awesome in the sims.
Know how the fuel balancing system works (C2101This man flew in the air force thunderbirds, so he will pump you up if you're doing aero sims.

C2203 and I2101: Honestly one of the nicest guys. He will really test your knowledge and go incredibly in depth but he wants you to learn and get better. Systems and details about procedures will help you.

Very relaxed and nice. Provides insight into different methods of the looking at material. Felt as though I performed slowly on EPs on sim but still gave 4s on everything. Still will ensure you know your material.
Awesome instructor. I learned a ton from him. Fair grader.

Come in, know your stuff as and ask him questions and it'll be a breeze. Super helpful and insightful in making sure a concept "clicks" for you. I dicked up an EP and he still graded generously because my brief was solid.

He is a decent instructor. I had him for a last block of instrument sims and he was upset that I didn't pull up NOTAMs, AHAS, TFR s and METARs/TAFs for OUR SIMULATOR EVENT. After that I flew a solid hop.

When it comes to altitudes in the High Altitude Penetration, he wants you at those altitudes at those DME points, I penetrated about 100-200 feet above the checkpoints and intercepted the ILS at the FAF, but he wants you hitting every step down.

C3101 &3202 Grades fairly but constantly talks loud as hell into the mic. Likes to grab the stick. Liked to bang on the OFT desk to "drive" points home. Brief was long as well 40&50 min respectively. Didn't learn much, was more annoyed than anything and just wanted to leave. Mostly 4s with some 3s.

Had him for 2102 and 2202. He has a ton of knowledge about the aircraft and aviation and in general. Bring questions to the brief, and as long as he is feeling nice that day, you'll do fine. Likes to coach a lot during the sim, which some may like and others may not.
FAM2102: gave me EP's back to back to back. Very good instructor def is into coaching students. RIPS cigs lol, cool guy
Great instructor, really cares about your understanding of the material and your success. Chill, but very informational.

FAM2201: Super nice dude, same info as above, very helpful and likes to make sure you understand what you're doing instead of just following checklists. Know some info about your flight gear if you're doing 2101-2202, asked me about knife and radio locations while I was suiting up.
^^ to the ciggies, pulled out his Marlboro golds and told me the smoke/fume EP was because he was puffing in the backseat

One of the few sim instructors I've had that doesn't seem to like his job. Came across as disinterested/bored during both the brief and sim, no sense of hur, maybe I caught him on a bad day. Brief questions/sim were not particularly difficult, but seems to be new to the syllabus. Fair grader despite.
This dude is pretty chill in my experience
Agree with the first review - very dry, not enthusiastic. Doesn't ask many questions to gauge your knowledge, nor does he offer many useful pieces of information to help you out in the future.
He is for sure chill and just be prepared to take the lead. Likely won't ask you a lot of questions.

Agree with above. Chill but seemed bored for a lot of it, which is fair since it was the I2200. But if you ask him questions about his flying days, he starts talking a little re. Fair grader and not a tough briefer

Definitely doesn't seem to be the most enthusiastic about his job, but he isn't as bad as the above has made him out to be. Ask him a question about his career or past experiences and he will open up a bit.
Fam2201 - Started late and ended early, never put in grades online. Def gotta ask questions to pull it outta him, USMC Huey guy. Was in for a long time does not give a fuck but cool guy.

He will ask you random information off ATIS. Pop circuit breakers, and give start up malfunctions just for fun. Just keep a watchful eye. - Will hit you with EP's that aren't even graded for the day to get your mind cranking.
C2201: Very informative, helpful, explained a lot of background info and tips for EPs. Likes you to set

33% torque @ 150 KIAS for st EPs that don't require PCL OFF or IDLE. Have intelligent questions for him, he likes to explain the procedures in depth and if you show that you have good questions he will like that. During the actual sim he would freeze the screen and let me go through the non-critical achtion items from the pocket checklist. Anticipate the next EP you are doing and try to have the right actions ready to go.

Nearly the exact same description for C3201, except he didn't pull circuit breakers or ask ATIS info from me. We remained focused on PEL/ELP causes. He likes to make sure you set 4-6% torque when reducing power for glide, and will comment when you stray from it, as well as when you stray the pipper from the izon during gliding
Watch out for Cockpit Alt during your climb checks. He likes to depressurize the cockpit.
Big on ATIS in instruments, has good reasoning on st of his quirks. Man really does like to talk and share stories, pencil out some time after your brief.

C3202: He lets you know what's coming before he does it, so he expects you react rather quickly. If something doesn't sound right, just turn it back toward North Field. He'll use personal stories to illustrate that if it doesn't sound right then get back home quick.

I2101- will ask you about the and Spoke but will additionally ask about each cross check instrument for the nose wing and performance, really means business be prepared to answer a lot of questions. Also does a million OPS Checks and will give you the Transducer and Cockpit ALT overpressurization to actually make sure you are checking your engine instruments.
Know what each of the engine instruments are actually indicating, even for early flights. For my C2102 he asked how each of them relate to the fire triangle for starting the engine.

I3103: Pretty quiet, but very nice. He's a reservist still instructing with VT-3 so he is on top of what it's like to actually go out and fly and will conduct the sim without too many "sim-isms." Won't correct you if you miss something until the last second so you have a chance to correct your own mistakes. Fair grader, and will set you up for success throughout the event.
I3103: Super nice guy, really helpful with questions. Cool during the sim even when you make mistakes, debrief was helpful and prepared me well for the next sim

June 2024 - he is no longer a reservist from what I gathered. That being said, the sim was similar to flying with a "chill" instructor in the plane. He lets you fly without a lot of input, will let you make small mistakes to learn from yourself before telling you exactly what to do which is nice later in training. Very nice guy!

Prior enlisted and went P3. Trains very in depth and gives explanations regarding why you would do something. Will let you screw up so you can see how the plane reacts then he will reset and let you try it again. Overall great instructor

Had him for C2202. Very helpful. If you do well in the brief, he'll help you out in the sim. Paused the OFT a bunch so we could talk about what I was seeing in the cockpit as well as make sure I had no questions about the procedures/techniques involved. Great instructor.

C2201: One of my favorites, definitely loves it if you know your stuff. Just regurgitate the EPs then talk through the nuances (not vice versa). Created the malfunction flow chart that you're given at book issue. Post debrief loves to bs, so ask him some questions. He will absolutely teach you a few things to take with you in your career.
3101: Enthusiastic, if you studied your material and know what is going on, he will assist and coach you through the brief and sim. Enjoyable Instructor.
Kinda slow talking. Usually a friendly guy and pretty timid
Likes to instruct during sims, but because he talks a little slow it can disrupt your flow
His back has been in pain recently (8/13/18), but even in pain he was still not harsh
Good dude, had a really good way of explaining the S-1 which was better than T6-B Driver. Very smart and likes to talk about helos.
Has a daughter in her mid 20's wanting to go to school for Petroleum Engineering, his daughter wants to get a job out west.
They love it out west like in Colorado, the untains, outdoors, good dude.
Impress him in the brief and the sim will be cake. He talks over you and t alks a lot in the sim so be ready for that. It was enjoyable to fly with him because he cares so much about you learning.

Have questions ready for the brief, our brief lasted ~10 minutes and then he asked if I had any questions, and I only had one. He seemed pretty disappointed and after every topic we covered in the debrief, he asked if I had any questions and seemed disappointed when I didn't.

C2101-- overall nice guy, recently retired from being an IP (May 2019), gave good advice and a realistic feeling of what it is like to have an IP. Since it was my first sim he was pretty generous. Come prepared, he didn't ask me many questions but was pleasantly surprised when I knew answers. Know the actions column for checklist.

I2104 Reasonable and down to earth. Actually teaches you and lets you fly, then makes comments. Did well so we worked ahead. My kind of instructor, not too much yapping, talks when necessary. Hope I have him again.
Asked a bunch of questions during the brief and had high expectations, but was a fair grader
If you have him for an EP sim, know the notes, warnings, and cautions that go along with the EP. He will be super impressed and probably give you a 5

C2101: He will walk you over to the ejection sequence/IROK procedures board in the front of the entrance to the sim bay and walk you through the whole ejection process, so if you see know everything about it he will be super impressed.
C2102: Asked about every component on the ejection seat sequence and components. Know your numbers and ch yuh ecklists. Fair grader
C2202: He asked way re systems questions than the other 4 instructors I've had so far. But if you know the answers, he helps you out a lot with the sim part.

C3101- High expectations in the brief. Knows the FTI very well so you can't BS him. I still wound up having a good brief. In the sim, he let me get completely through a maneuver before applying feedback, gave his feedback, and often let me try the maneuver again (stall, spin, etc). His grade for the maneuver was based off the better of the 2. Know the maneuvers cold and he will help you with the flying part.
I2203: asked a lot of questions about anything that had a number in the briefing guide. Only gave 3's if you were 100' off alt

FAM2202 - Dont know if it's te same McNeal but guy i got was a AV-8Bpilot, southern guy. Big on systems numbers related to EP's for hydraulic system and OBOGS. Overall gave good feedback and very helpful def a detail oriented jet type guy.
From Ohio, likes sports, real chill
Good, helps you through a good aunt

I2103. I had a rible start to my sim because I was having an off day. He coached me through, helped me focus and chill out, and then I did well. He's incredibly helpful, and super nice.

Excellent Instructor, very chill yet knowledgeable about the sim. Will give you time to make mistakes and correct, big on basic air work for instrument sims. I botched one of the steep turns and he had me roll it out and try it again, saying "That's not how I expected you to perform that, we won't count that one." He didn't ask many brief questions at all, just top of the waves stuff. Not a fan of the FTI procedures for unusual attitudes and scan techniques, he will give you his personal tips which tend to work much better.
Really great instructor, and patient with you
Very nice guy. Doesn't over react or stress you out.

Great instructor. Actually tries to get to know you before the brief. Had him for the first BI sim and as long as you know the FTI steps for the procedures cold he is willing to do a lot of coaching on steep turns, timed turns, etc.

Was my ground school instructor, very helpful and good at explanations. He understands the struggle and mentioned to our class that he's only ever failed a kid because they were just a shitbag. Super nice.
Excellent instructor, very laid back and helpful if you know your stuff going into the brief. Big on maintaining a great energy throughout

FAM6101 - good instructor, asked questions on all departure procedures for NSE2V and VFR departure (difference on directions and calls). Asked about 4 A's and ABCDONT and OLF procedures and Jay course rules back to landing RW 32 via Easy. Walked us through it for the most part during the sim. Mostly an majintro into actually flying course rules

Very long brief, lots of pauses for fill in the blank numbers. Solid flight, big on OPS checks, tells you when to do them but then writes in grades that he prompted you. Real big on manipulating the PCL. Brutal debrief, the guy doesn't forget a single thing. Made a big deal out small things, grade sheet loaded with comments

Very nice guy, I had him for C2103. If you know your stuff hes very helpful and grades you very favorably. If you are very proficient he has no problem helping you practice for your next sim. He also has a lot of good technique points he makes throughout alst every part of the event. I hope to get him again.
Pretty cool for VNAV, spends a lot of time talking in the brief clearing up lots of gotcha's on the chart study. Know you stuff and come well prepared.
You will learn, but it will be on his schedule. He is pretty long winded and the brief can get a little painful at times, but he genuinely wants you to learn and he will teach you his methods.

Incredibly helpful, overly knowledgeable of the T-6, will set you up for success throughout the sim. Allows you mess up, shows you how to fix it, lets you try it again, and then grades you off the second attempt. All he wants to see is that you're taking his advice and applying it.
Really enjoyed this Cooley. Yes, he is long winded, but everything he mentions is pertinent to the sim and your knowledge. Enjoy him. Very charismatic.

He's alright, he's really about Anti FOD, talks about how not to FOD the aircraft for about 5 minutes. But overall as long as you know your stuff he's pretty chill. Doesn't really say if you're doing something wrong or if there was a better way of doing a procedure till the end during the debrief; may be kinda hard to gauge if the SIM is going well for you. He definitely did re talking than st instructors about the subjects that the briefing guide goes over.

I2103: expects you to lead the sim. He doesn't want students to get used to being "sandbags" in the cockpit so he had me lay out the plan for the sim and then once we got there he was completely hands off and just observed. The brief for I2103 is basically the approach pattern and unusual attitudes, but he had USN going through briefing guides for later instrument sims showing me what we were "supposed" to be doing and this was a little over the top. The sim itself went fine but it is very hard to gauge how you are doing and he will not say much.

He gives fair/good grades but mannnn is this dude over the top. For I2103 he started briefing the nearest airfield and ejection areas as well as which radio settings belong to the nearest OLFs. He'll give you the lead on the sim and will not say anything about what maneuver to do next. Write down the order before when you brief it so that you have it on your kneeboard in the sim. Also do ops checks after every maneuver, he's huge on those.

He's an odd dude. I don't really like him because he acts like you're doing everything well and then during the debrief he tears you apart. That being said, he grades well. He wants things done his way but doesn't tell you what that is until the debrief and then acts like you should have known (I did things by the FTI and NATOPs for C2201)

C2101 He spent 30 min going over the differences between the front and the rear cockpit, and quizzing as he went. His level of detail can come across as a bit extreme, he gave me an abnormal cockpit and then asked me what was wrong. (Probes anti ice was on, and Air Cond) Overall, seems fair just be ready to play his game, take notes, and smile and you will be fine.

Agree with all of the above. For C2201 I would know the controlled ejection sites and know the NATOPs pocket checklist cold, as in where to find each EP. During the sim he will freeze it and allow you to do the EP which was pretty nice. Also when you hand over controls make sure your feet are completely off of the rudder pedals, he will hit you on that.

Had him for 3102 and hit me with questions about OLF and working area presets which I was unprepared for so he gave me MIF on communications. His briefs are re in depth than any other instructor I've had thus far. He's not a generous grader.

I2104 Worst instructor I've had so far, expects you to have a flight profile and brief as if we are actually going to the plane. Don't forget anything before you go into the sim (like a chart or a profile index card), that is a huge pet peeve of his. If you got a 5 on a previous event (unless you think you can crush it again), he says you shouldn't do the maneuver again (told me this in the debrief after I jacked up my steep turn). DOES NOT SAY A WORD during the actual sim so its hard to tell how its going for you. Will blast you in the st round about ways during the debrief. He literally spent 45 minutes of the debrief telling me about some space mission, how he left his keys at the grocery store, and how he has a beach house and 3 cars just to tell me I jacked things up in the sim instead of just flat out telling me what I did wrong. Oh and he was talking crap about the other instructors and how they like to actually talk with us as humans and get to know us a little bit. That guy probably couldn't have even told you what my name was 5 minutes after the event if you asked him.

C2101. Know the checklists verbatim and especially the notes under each action and details as well as what you're looking for on the items. Dudes by the book but frankly we all should be too. If you've got 2101 with him know where stuff is by mery and to recall it when he goes over the differences between fore and aft cockpits, its actually useful. Wasn't overly critical but corrected me when I missed stuff or misspoke but left little issues like saying "switch" alone. Debrief had good feedback of a few points to learn/correct and how to be better next time. Hes critical of people who are lax, but being a rubber stamp doesn't make anyone better.
C2103: A little bit awkward. Talked a lot about the pocket checklist and differences between front and aft cockpit. Nice guy. Had no real issues. Was tough on the debrief. He's a talker.
Right after you're cleared for takeoff, he'll ALWAYS put an aircraft coming in to land on your runway, just to see if you're really clearing left, right, and above.

I2101 - A CH-53E guy and prior VT-2 instructor. Overall a really cool and relaxed dude and really helpful in his coaching during the sim portion. During the brief he will bring up the discussion points, test your knowledge of the procedure, then give his own personal experience with how the T-6 will respond in both the sim and on the flightline. If there is extra time, he will put you through other procedures outside the current sim and give you some extra experience to broaden your SA.

Really enjoyed my sim with him. He's very friendly, personable, and funny. We talked a lot about his daughter. Had him for C2201. He used to teach systems. This man loves systems. Not in a bad way that he is nagging you with questions but, he enjoys talking about the systems related to your sim and getting into how it works and why certain thing's work the way they do. For C2201 he told me exactly what ep's were coming and had me frozen so I could perform the ep without worrying about airwork. Learned a lot from him. Pretty sure he's one of the guys that created T6Bdriver, so I a recommend knowing everything t6bdriver says about your sim. My favorite instructor so far.

For 2102, know that there are seven abnormal starts. Know your critical action items. All in all he's a very funny and positive instructor. If you come prepared, he'll help you out and tell you some tricks that I thought was helpful.
For 2103 know your systems. As for the sim, it was very informational aka he would give a GEN warning and just have me look at what systems were lost. Didn't actually have to perform any procedures

Had him for C2201. Great instructor. He really helped to hammer home systems. He would freeze me so we could look at and talk through the indications that I was seeing. The above comments about t6b driver are correct, he walked me through the exact same decision tree listed on there. He'll help lead you to some of the answers but I think he enjoyed going into the weeds with me.
I3104: Probably the best instructor I've had yet. He gave a lot of tips on how to keep track of everything during an approach. Really enjoyable to learn from.

C2102: His voice should be familiar to you because he's the guy who narrates st (if not all) of the T6-B driver videos. That being said, know everything in the videos related to your sim and brief. I did that and had a great event, learned a ton and got good grades. Definitely someone to hope for sims with.

C2101: Good instructor but can only speak to what he is like for the very early sims. Super nice, friendly, straightforward guy who just recently came from the North Field flightline. Not really funny, but not not funny if that makes sense. Led the brief but that might just be because it was the first sim. Asked a few basic knowledge questions, nothing crazy. Didn't throw me any curveballs at me but then again it was the first sim. Puts a TON of emphasis on accuracy over speed with regards to the checklist, but don't just crawl through the checklist. Also puts emphasis on knowing the radio calls. If you know your stuff, he will take notice; he's a fair grader. He drops a few nuggets of knowledge but also lets you get through the sim. If you finish early, he likes to see how much more you know beyond the sim requirements, which is a good opportunity to get better grades and advice on things further down the syllabus.

C2102: A pretty nice guy who did 2 tours as an instructor at TW-5 and definitely enjoys teaching. Pretty much did the entire brief, just asking me a few questions along the way. He talked a lot about the general methods to handling EP's from the FTI. With all of the EP's in this sim being on the ground, he really emphasized the first priority - maintaining control of the aircraft, especially with the fire warning light. Just some general EP advice, focus initially on that first priority and then take a few seconds to analyze the situation and see if there are other indications that verify the warning you received instead of "fast-handing" it and immediately running through the actions.

C2201: Pretty nice guy, stresses knowing the FWOP like crazy. Make sure for in flight EPs, you know to control the aircraft first, which he likes to say is very "situationally dependent." Didn't get above 3500ft and would throw 2-3 malfunctions back to back. Didn't really let me even work all the way through one to see the process. All that to say, Mostly 4s with a couple 3s.

I2101 - Pretty much told me I'm too stupid to fly fixed wing lol, "destined to fly helos" was the exact verbiage. Def has high standards. Made me write the whole flight profile of maneuvers. Just gotta have thick skin. Just gotta go really into detail when preparing for sims, especially if you have him for any sim where you're graded on flying. Didn't rip me on grades so that's nice and was almost complete silent during the sim. 3.6/10 would not recommend

Fam3101 - good instructor, will ask you about each maneuver in the briefing guide and why you don't use relax, max, level ball for everything. Wasn't super strict on the maneuvers but did make me do one or two twice to be better. Did talk me through sticking points during the sim and graded fairly, cool guy was in the navy. Just study the maneuvers from the FTI and gouge and you will be fine.

Fam 6102 - USMC c-130 guy. Has a cool haircut, asked about outbound VFR course rules to do touch n go RW 090 @ Barin and asked about all course rules back in to a straight in RW 14 at home field pretty straight forward sim, cool chill guy.
Boy does he love to talk about fishing.

I studied pretty hard for my sim all for him to sit and talk for almost 40 minutes straight before we got in the sim. I never even said a word. Then when we got in the sim he was super picky. Never really let me show him what I knew and gave me average grades.

I hate this guy. Even if you know your stuff on him being a jerk for no reason. Also don't plan on getting and tips or pointers or even constructive criticism. He doesn't grade hard but it's just not fun to have a sim with him.

He will probably talk for the whole brief. I knew my stuff well but was just smiling and nodding for st of it. He was 10 minutes late, took a full half hour in the brief, and then took a 10 minute bathroom break. In the sim you have to initiate it if you want to do anything (ie, ask to do a maneuver) I think I could have just done circles around the A for the full time if I didn't step in and say stuff. I thought he coached me on the PEL pretty well though.

He likes to talk and you probably won't get a chance to show that you studied in the brief. When you have him as an instructor, it'll probably feel like you're by yourself for the st part because he doesn't talk much, he's watching how you handle things and perform. He's a consistent grader, I've had him twice and both times I got all 4's.

Accurate comments above, he's not a particularly enjoyable sim. Doesn't ask much for questions, when he does I couldn't tell if he understood what I said or not. He asks you if you have questions about 20 times during the brief, uncomfortably long pauses at times and he scrolls aimlessly thru the briefing guide. I think he's about half deaf, which could contribute to this. Starts late, then has a bathroom break and then ended late. Bit of a yeller in the sim, no hope of him pausing it to discuss anything. Mostly 4's on grades, pretty useless debrief.

Really nice man, but my experience was pretty consistent with the previous comments for C2101. He talked at me the entire brief and explained the discuss items instead of asking me. The time in the sim was pretty uneventful. Nice man and patient, which was greatly appreciated for my first sim. All in all, not a bad instructor to be assigned.

C2103: Quiet, but good instructor. He does st of the speaking, but when opportunities present themselves, insert your NATOPS knowledge. He'll appreciate that. If you finish your checklists early, he'll just silently sit there, and let you fly around for practice. He didn't care too much about coms. Nice man, and I enjoyed my sim with him.

Decent guy, but definitely half deaf. Visible hearing aid in ear. I had to call "below 150, gear" 5 times (loudly) in I3106 for him to hear it, then was critiqued for lowering gear and going to BAC late.

He was re interested in randomly yelling at me, talking to other instructors halfway through my sim, than actually helping me. He also fell asleep halfway through another students sim. Other than that he's a decent person.

"CANCEL THE MASTER WARNINGS AND CAUTIONS." Also won't respond to "Gear down" and "Flaps - ___" on Before Landing checklist on a landing pattern sim. Also continually ate candy over the ICS. Otherwise, he didn't say anything so it was basically a practice sim. Learned nothing

I2102- Excellent instructor, straight chiller. Don't suck or be stupid and you will be 100% fine. Former F-18 guy who has great insight into how to fly a fixed wing plane when the FTI was written by helo bubbas. Fly the VSI!
